questions.q: What does GROUP BY Color do before AVG(ListPrice) runs?
options: Splits the table into one group per distinct Color value
Deletes rows with duplicate colors
Sorts the table by Color, with no other effect
Removes the Color column from the results
questions.explain: GROUP BY partitions rows into groups sharing the same value(s), and aggregates run separately within each group.

questions.q: How many rows does 'SELECT Color, AVG(ListPrice) FROM Production.Product GROUP BY Color;' return?
options: One row per distinct Color value
One row total, for the whole table
One row per product
Zero rows, since this is invalid syntax
questions.explain: GROUP BY collapses each group down to one summary row — same row count as SELECT DISTINCT Color would produce.

questions.q: Why does 'SELECT Name, Color, AVG(ListPrice) FROM Production.Product GROUP BY Color;' fail?
options: Name isn't aggregated and isn't in GROUP BY, so there's no single unambiguous Name per Color group
AVG cannot be combined with GROUP BY under any circumstances
Color must always be aggregated too
GROUP BY can only be used with one column in the SELECT list
questions.explain: Since multiple products (with different names) share a Color, SQL Server has no single Name to display per group.

questions.q: What are the two valid options for a column listed in SELECT when GROUP BY is used?
options: It must be wrapped in an aggregate function, or listed in GROUP BY itself
It must always be the primary key
It must be a text column, never numeric
It must appear in the WHERE clause
questions.explain: This is the core GROUP BY rule — every non-aggregated SELECT column needs to be part of the grouping.

questions.q: What are the three conceptual steps of GROUP BY?
options: Split into groups, aggregate within each group, combine into one row per group
Filter, sort, and limit
Join, filter, and sort
Count, sum, and average, in that fixed order
questions.explain: This split/aggregate/combine mental model explains why GROUP BY behaves the way it does.
